Lessons.Title: Survey the Class, Survey the School
ExplanationParagraphs: Original First Edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 8 Lesson 6 is a real-world CATEGORICAL SURVEY and collection task. Local teacher HTML and preparation read. The two source images are a favorite-science-topic graph and blank results-table reference; their pixels and the separately described blackline master were not individually inspected. These visual resources remain teacher-linked, not embedded.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: Survey (10 minutes). With a partner inspect the original bar graph and propose categories, such as living things, space, ecosystems, weather and energy, rather than inferring exact counts from unverified pixels. Every bar names an answer category; bar length/height represents count, not a new question.

Activity 1 Create a Survey (10 minutes). Teams of FOUR design ONE specific, understandable categorical survey question with UP TO SIX clear, preferably mutually exclusive answer choices. Review whether respondents can select one category without confusion. Revise the question after peer feedback. The original survey is authentic, not a prefabricated numerical dataset.

Activity 2 Survey a Large Group (25-minute lesson block plus possible 2–3 days across school). Teams of FOUR plan who will present the survey and answer choices, who will record responses, and how to prevent COUNTING THE SAME STUDENT MULTIPLE TIMES. Use the original source blank recording table if available or lined paper. Collect actual responses, including possibly another class, with teacher permission and privacy requirements.

Survey data gathered now will be used in the NEXT lesson to make a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph. Keep exact category labels and original observed counts; do not fabricate school results to complete the follow-up graph. If no school survey occurs, label any practice frequencies explicitly as invented and avoid claiming they represent a real response sample.

An INDEPENDENT first-party rehearsal can illustrate tally logic only: choose a fictional preferred reading topic and imagine 3, 5, 2 responses across three clear categories, a total of 10. These example data must never overwrite the authentic class survey, which remains dependent on observed individual responses.

Teacher synthesis: check every category is connected to the survey prompt, responses are counted once, and each question has a recorded data collection plan. Students explain surprises and observations. Original publisher Reflect on Collecting Data Cool-down is gated and not copied. Tests authored but runtime/Stage D and academic signoff unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Categorical survey
KeyConcepts.Definition: A question that groups responses into named answer categories.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use one question with up to six distinct choices.

KeyConcepts.Title: Authentic frequency
KeyConcepts.Definition: The tally is the actual number of different respondents who chose a category.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count each respondent only once and preserve precise category totals.
KeyConcepts.Example: Fictional independent demonstration 3+5+2=10; not school data.

KeyConcepts.Title: Later reuse
KeyConcepts.Definition: The next lesson will graph the original collected categories and counts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not substitute invented numbers for the authentic source survey.
KeyConcepts.Example: Keep written counts and labels for each category.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent tally demonstration
WorkedExamples.Question: In an invented three-category practice, 3 choose space, 5 choose animals, 2 choose weather. How many DIFFERENT people responded?
Steps: Use a single response per person.
Keep these data separate from the actual school survey.
WorkedExamples.Check: If one respondent counted twice, the observed sample total must be corrected by teacher review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent mutually exclusive survey example
WorkedExamples.Question: Create a one-answer question with three independent response categories.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent first-party source-aligned reasoning; not a copy of the publisher's original image or student-authored work
Steps: Ask each participant to choose exactly one of Space, Animals or Weather.
Record fictional trial responses as 3, 5 and 2 (do not claim real class tallies).
Sum 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 and verify exactly one recorded category per participant.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 10 hypothetical responses; teacher reviews the real class/school questionnaire.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher separately checks the original source, pupil drawing or physical activity; this illustration is not an original-source parity certificate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check invented frequency labels
WorkedExamples.Question: For a fictional school interest survey, what is the difference between Animals (5) and Weather (2) responses?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independent first-party source-aligned reasoning; not a copy of the publisher's original image or student-authored work
Steps: Confirm both counts belong to one invented survey with the same respondent population.
Explain that a genuine Grade 3 survey requires actual consent, responses and teacher checks.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher separately checks the original source, pupil drawing or physical activity; this illustration is not an original-source parity certificate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: More than six choices or ambiguous overlapping choices.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source requires up to six answer choices in a clear categorical survey.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Revise categories and fit at most six.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Observed frequency inflation corrupts the later graph.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Track one response per participant without exposing sensitive personal identifiers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Invent frequencies for the school survey.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original 2021 activity requires an authentic large-group survey.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record real results; fictional sample is only labelled practice.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Guess bar heights from unverified published images.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source image values have not been pixel inspected.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use original source graph with the teacher.

SummaryPoints: Pair warm-up notice and wonder about survey categories.
Teams of four design a survey with up to six clear responses.
Record actual large-group data; prevent duplicate student counts.
Retain data and labels for next lesson scaled graphs.
Source blackline/PDF image pixels and gated publisher Cool-down are unverified.
